appraisal_events.evidence: son visage gluant se gâter ; comme un sirop qui tourne... Sa bouche devenait amère; then, revived by flattery, she asks « Qui ça ? » dans un intérêt naïf et gourmand, and « qui que ce fût, elle était heureuse ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator lowers Andrée twice over in one continuous movement: her face curdles with envy at hearing that others like him, and she is then restored to gaiety by any praise whatever, which exposes her good humour as vanity the narrator can switch on at will.

appraisal_events.evidence: Albertine avait pour toutes ces jolies choses un goût bien plus vif que la duchesse, and the fine things take on for her une importance, un charme qu'ils n'avaient certes pas pour la duchesse, rassasiée avant même d'être en état d'appétit.
appraisal_events.explanation: The last two paragraphs stage an explicit comparison in which Albertine's desire-sharpened, detailed knowledge of clothes is ranked above the satiated indifference of the duchesse de Guermantes and of rich women generally.

status_effects.explanation: Andrée comes off worse locally: her souring at a rival's good fortune and her indiscriminate hunger for praise are narrated as defects of character.
Albertine is locally elevated as the possessor of true, appetitive connoisseurship, explicitly rated above a duchess in the register the passage cares about.

The duchesse is the losing term of the comparison: named as sated before she can even feel appetite, and assimilated to bored museum-goers, while she is also reduced to a mere source of dressmaking information.

ambiguities: Albertine's elevation is grounded in her poverty and in clothes the narrator has had made for her (the shoes are read as signs qu'elle habitait chez moi), so the same paragraphs that raise her taste also mark her economic dependence; the dominant local movement is still the comparative elevation, but a reading that treats it as backhanded is available.

The whole passage is in the iterative imperfect (je voyais, disais-je, elle était heureuse), so these are habitual patterns rather than a single staged occasion; the events are best read as characterizing rather than as discrete incidents.
